description: Hacker Mates – San Luis & Villa Mercedes, Argentina. 2025 San Luis local winners and Global Nominees. This year we take on Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data, with a science-backed project on water, crops and farmers in the Argentine Pampas. We are five: a mechatronics engineer, two software technicians, a programming student and a data specialist.
summary: NAPA shows a farmer in the Argentine Pampas the water beneath their field, and how much their flood risk changes with what they plant. Here, floods don’t fall from the sky: they rise from the water table. In 2001 the flood covered 1.2 million hectares, took almost two years to recede and left US$700 million in losses. Yet farmers still choose what to plant by looking at the sky, and measure the soil with an auger: a single point, a single day. With 25 years of NASA data and a model tested blind against a real flood, NAPA gives the farmer their field’s water memory, the level of their area’s “tank” and seven rotation suggestions. Under the same 2001–03 rainfall, the model gives 9 flooded months with soybean–corn and 2 with alfalfa pasture. One field can’t stop a flood. A whole basin can.
details:
What exactly does it do?

NAPA is a decision-support system for choosing what to plant, built for a region where floods rise from the water table (napa, in Argentine Spanish). Specifically, it:

  • Shows each field’s water memory. The farmer draws their field and sees when and for how long each 30 m cell was under water, from 1984 to 2021 (Landsat).
  • Measures how full the area’s “tank” is today, compared with its own 2002–2024 history (GRACE/GRACE-FO, MODIS, GPM IMERG).
  • Suggests seven crop rotations, ranked by how many months they leave the field flooded and compared with the current one (GPM IMERG, NASA POWER).
  • Shows why to trust it: its validation numbers, side by side with the published ones.

The main result: under the same 2001–03 rainfall, soybean–corn leaves the field flooded for 9 months, and a rotation with alfalfa pasture for 2.

Figure 1. The soil in cross-section: where the water table sits under each rotation. A model scenario, not a forecast.

How does it work?

The region works like a tank. Over 50 years, annual crops replaced deep-rooted pastures and the water table rose from 6–12 m deep to 0–4 m (Houspanossian et al., 2023). The landscape filled the tank, rain makes it overflow, and the rotation decides how long the flood lasts.

  1. Observe. 25 years of monthly NASA data: surface water (MODIS), rainfall (GPM IMERG), stored water (GRACE/GRACE-FO) and evaporation demand (NASA POWER).
  2. Simulate. A monthly water balance: last month’s water, minus slow drainage, plus rain, minus what soil and crops evaporate. A month counts as flooded when the tank is more than 100 mm above normal.
  3. Compare. We run the tank once per rotation, with the same rain and each crop’s water use (FAO-56).
  4. Validate. We calibrated on the 2001–03 flood and tested blind on the 2012–13 flood: the model tracked the satellite record (rank correlation 0.85). We also reproduced 9 of the 11 results published by Kuppel et al. (2015).

Figure 2. The full path: which NASA data goes in, what the model computes, and what the farmer gets.

Limits we declare: a single field does not change the region’s water table; the effect needs the whole area. The second flood matches the published record less closely (peak of 16.1% versus 22.0%). The series ends in September 2025.

What did we discover?

It wasn’t El Niño. The two major floods began in neutral years, and during the three strong El Niño events of the period there was almost no surface water.

What floods the Pampas is accumulated rain: each season’s peak follows the rainfall of the three previous seasons (correlation 0.64) and barely follows the El Niño index (0.08). That is why NAPA watches the tank, not the forecast.

Figure 3. 25 years of surface water, month by month, with each season’s El Niño phase below.

What benefits does it have?

  • For the farmer. Today they choose what to plant by looking at the sky, and measure the soil with an auger: a single point, a single day. With NAPA they see the whole field and their area’s tank before planting. Two agronomists and a farm owner from the region confirmed that none of them has water-table data for their own land.
  • For the soil. Flooding is soil damage: waterlogged roots run out of oxygen, and a shallow water table carries salts up to the surface. A rotation that leaves the field flooded for fewer months protects soil health.
  • For the region. 3,854 farms on 2.6 million hectares across 11 districts (INDEC, 2018). The 2001 flood covered 1.2 million hectares, left 10,686 farmers under agricultural emergency and caused US$700 million in losses (Scarpati et al., 2008).
  • For the basin. One field can’t stop a flood. A whole basin can: in our model, with alfalfa pasture across the area, the 2001–03 flood goes from 9 flooded months to 2.
  • In dry years. The same water table that floods is a water reserve when rain fails: where it stays within reach of the roots, crops can draw on it. So the tank level matters in both extremes: flood and water shortage.

What do we hope to achieve?

  • Now. The tank is filling again: in September 2025 it was 139 mm above normal; one month before the 2001 peak, it was 162. We want the next flood to be seen coming.
  • In one year. A pilot with farmers, agronomists and INTA extension staff, and the whole region at 30 m with up-to-date data during the 2026/27 El Niño.
  • After that. Other plains: the same mechanism is documented in the US Midwest (Zhang and Schilling, 2006), and the method transfers by recalibrating drainage and the flooding threshold.

You can’t choose the rain. You can choose what you plant.

What tools did we use?

  • Data: NASA MODIS, GPM IMERG, GRACE/GRACE-FO, NASA POWER and Landsat, plus NASA GIBS layers.
  • Analysis: Python, Earth Engine API, pandas, NumPy, SciPy and pytest.
  • Web: React, Vite, Leaflet, Leaflet-Geoman, Turf.js, Recharts and Supabase, with tests in Vitest and Playwright.
